newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Krupp chief booed by angry steel workers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Krupp chief booed by angry steel workers.

text.p: Angry German steel workers, fearing large-scale job cuts, on Tuesday pelted the chairman of steel giant Krupp with eggs and oranges in protest against the company's hostile takeover bid of its larger rival Thyssen AG.

"Where is the killer?" and "String him up!", Thyssen workers chanted as riot police blocked their attempt to storm Krupp's headquarters to confront boss Gerhard Cromme -- blamed by unions for closing down steel plants after previous takeovers.

Thousands of steel workers laid down their tools on Tuesday to protest against the bid amid fears that a giant merger in Germany's Ruhr Valley industrial heartland could cost thousands of workers their jobs.
The plan looked set to spark a new wave of protests only days after miners virtually paralysed the German capital Bonn in protest against coal subsidy cuts.

Between 2,000 and 3,000 steel workers, mainly from Thyssen, massed outside the headquarters of Krupp in the western city of Essen after Thyssen said late on Monday it had information Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp planned a hostile takeover bid.

The IG Metall metal workers union, Germany's biggest union, called on steel workers to mount overnight vigils at the gates of steel plants at least until an assembly of steel workers on Wednesday and left open the possibility of further protests.
Holger Hollnack, a member of the Thyssen Stahl AG works council of employers and unions, said steel output at Thyssen was cut to half on Tuesday by the protests.
Thyssen management said the merger could only be carried out with "tens of thousands" of job cuts in the steel industry.
Thousands of Thyssen workers came to Essen in buses and cars. Some held banners proclaiming: "If Cromme comes to power, we won't have a future".
Cromme, dubbed by the metalworker's union as the "Ruhr's number one jobs killer", eventually came out of his office to face the angry crowd that pelted him with eggs and oranges.
Speaking from behind a bullet-proof screen, he told them rumours of impending job cuts were nonsense but he did not say whether his company was going ahead with the bid for Thyssen.
That news came later on Tuesday, when Krupp confirmed plans to takeover Thyssen and said it was confident it would succeed.
"The numbers making the rounds are pure panic-mongering," said Cromme, who was booed by protesters.
Krupp offered to pay Thyssen shareholders 435 marks a share for the company's stock, a premium of 25 percent over Monday's closing share price.
IG Metall attacked Cromme in a statement saying he already had a reputation for being "unscrupulous" after steel works closures in the 1980s.
"It's no different to 10 years ago. Thousands of steel workers are not only scared of losing their jobs but also of poverty," IG Metall, Germany's biggest union, said.

One woman steelworker at the protest said she had worked for Hoesch before it was taken over by Krupp in 1991, she said: "Hoesch used to have three steel mills. Two are gone now and what are young people supposed to do."
A merger, if it went ahead, would create the third largest steel group in Europe in terms of output after British Steel and France's Usinor Sacilor SA.
With combined sales of more than 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion), a merged group would be better able to tackle overcapacity and could force its rivals to restructure too.
But, analysts said, the layoffs that would inevitably be part of the process would not go down well in the Ruhr Valley where unemployment is already high.
Steelworkers said they would take heart from the week of protests by miners that succeeded in securing concessions from the government over its plans to cut coal subsidies.
"We will not just sit back and let this happen to us. Basically this is undiluted capitalism, pure Wild West methods," Willy Siegerer, the deputy head of the Thyssen works council, told German radio.

Dieter Kroll, the head of Thyssen works council, told NRW radio earlier that both he and the head of Krupp's works council Werner Nass feared such a takeover could mean the loss of 10,000 jobs in the state of North-Rhine Westphalia.
Nass told NRW radio the merger could mean the loss of 5,500 to 6,000 jobs in the city of Dortmund alone and that this would mean an unemployment rate of about 20 percent there.

Thyssen's works council said it would be holding a series of meetings this week to discuss Krupp's plans and vowed to keep a round-the-clock protest outside the Thyssen steelworks at Hamborn-Beeckerwerh in the Ruhr.
